newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng Xiaoping - pragmatist who transformed China.
newsitem.headline: Deng Xiaoping - pragmatist who transformed China.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping, whose death was announced on Thursday, was China's great survivor, a pragmatist who bounced back from three ultra-left purges to enlist capitalist devices to shore up communist power.

He swept China out of an age stunted by Maoist ideological constraints and Stalinist central planning, pulling tens of millions of Chinese out of absolute poverty and opening up the opportunity to make or lose fortunes in a market economy.

However, the short man with a harsh gravelly voice who put televisions in peasants homes failed to offer his people a vision, leaving a nation of institutionalised cynicism in which money became the only source of values.
He allowed entrepreneurs to start private businesses, founded free-wheeling special economic zones and reopened stock markets closed by decades of communist austerity.
He did not permit freedom of expression or the rule of law not sanctioned by the Communist Party. He created a nation without guidance of law or spiritual principles.
Deng, the grand engineer of China's market-oriented economic reforms, was convinced only economic prosperity would save the Communist Party from the fate of its comrade in the former Soviet Union.
He allowed nothing to challenge either the party's grip on politics or his own plans for economic change, even long after he gave up official positions.

In 1989, when student-led pro-democracy demonstrations brought more than a million people into Beijing streets, Deng ordered army tanks and soldiers armed with live ammunition into Tiananmen Square to crush the unrest, no matter what the cost in lives.

Three years later, when the Communist Party leadership he helped to install in power dragged its feet on economic reforms, modern China's outstanding manipulator reemerged dramatically from retirement to force the government to follow his plan.
Unlike his political opponents, Deng was unhampered by worries about whether things such as stock markets or foreign investment were capitalist or socialist.

"It doesn't matter if the cat is black or white," he was quoted as arguing, "as long as it catches mice it is a good cat." That was the stuff of legend. In fact he had compared a black and a yellow cat, colleagues said in a 1997 government-sponsored television documentary on his life.

From the time he became China's unquestioned leader in 1978, Deng fought for reforms -- summarised by the slogan "to get rich is glorious" -- that freed the economy from its communist strait-jacket and unleashed an entrepreneurial spirit.
He abolished revolutionary Chairman Mao Zedong's agricultural communes -- vast, faceless collections of farmers working without hope of personal gain -- and let peasants enrich themselves.
City workers, too, were allowed to strive for a better life without fear of being condemned politically, and new businesses and free markets sprung up everywhere.
Deng opened China to Western business and investment.
Through it all Deng firmly resisted Western political ideas, however, demanding that China remain committed to "socialism with Chinese characteristics".
Deng once said socialism was "the only way for everyone to prosper".

Purged three times in power struggles in the 1930s and with radicals led by Mao's wife Jiang Qing in 1966 and 1976, Deng was hailed as a hero when he rebounded from political exile in 1977 to rescue China from the leftist excesses of Mao's 1966-76 Cultural Revolution.
After the army clampdown on June 4, 1989, Deng's people silently reviled him as one of the butchers of Beijing.
When he made his dramatic campaign against bureaucratic stagnation in 1992, he galvanised public imagination, winning admiration as the only man who could still change the course of China's history.
That last great campaign underlined one of his greatest failings -- his inability to pass the reins of real power to anyone else.

Deng's third hand-picked successor, Jiang Zemin, reelected as Communist Party chief at the 13th party congress in 1992 that elevated Deng's capitalist market economic theories to communist gospel, will take over a system in which Deng has failed to set in place mechanisms for a transfer of power.
He leaves his heir to almost certain factional warfare.
Jiang's two predecessors, Zhao Ziyang and Hu Yaobang, were both toppled by hardliners after outbreaks of unrest.
Zhao was purged in 1989, days after troops moved into Tiananmen Square and two year's after Deng's first protege, Hu, lost his position in a similar power struggle.
Deng, born in southwestern Sichuan province on August 22, 1904 to a small landlord and his concubine, was a chain smoker who enjoyed a drink until just a few years before he died.
Just five feet (1.5 metres) tall, Deng's non-conformist ideas made him stand out in a country where the safest course is usually just to repeat the party line.
Official publications said playing pool, a happy family and a sense of optimism were some secrets behind Deng's longevity.
His daughter Deng Lin said bridge, Beijing opera and soccer were her father's lifelong passions. He also had a penchant for white socks.

Deng allowed little to be known of his personal life, abhorring the cult of personality that surrounded Mao. He and his third wife Zhuo Lin had two sons and three daughters and several grandchildren. His first wife died and his second divorced him.
Deng's association with leftwing ideas began early in his life and from 1920 to 1925 he studied in France.

In 1926, he went to Moscow, returning to China the same year to play a minor role in the communist cause. He became a soldier and played a leading role in ultimately unsuccessfuly campaigns to liberate southwestern Guangxi region from Nationalist rule.
He took part in the historic 1934-35 Long March, the communists' arduous 6,000 mile (10,000 km) retreat on foot that defined a generation of revolutionary leadership.

He was elected to the central committee in 1945, helped to defeat the Nationalists on the battlefield and was given administrative responsibility over his native southwest after Mao declared the People's Republic of China in 1949.

In 1952, he was promoted to vice premier, became finance minister in 1953, a full member of the politburo in 1956 and remained in Mao's inner cabinet until he was first toppled from power at the start of Mao's Cultural Revolution.
Deng was humiliated as "the number two capitalist roader" (after then-president Liu Shaoqi) and purged in 1966. He spent the next few years as a worker in a factory in central Jiangxi province.
Persecuted by Red Guards, his elder son Deng Pufang threw himself from a window at Beijing University and was denied proper medical treatment, crippling him for life.

Deng resurfaced from political oblivion as a vice-premier in 1973 and took control of the government in 1974 when Premier Zhou Enlai was found to have cancer. It was then that he, and Zhou, began to introduce the economic reforms that were later to transform China.
In 1976, he was stripped of his posts again after the Tiananmen incident -- a mass demonstration to mourn the death of Zhou that was violently broken up by security forces.
Deng was attacked as an instigator by Mao's wife who was trying to consolidate her own power as Mao lay dying.

After Mao's death and the dramatic arrest of Jiang's "Gang of Four", Deng bounced back in 1977 to be absolved of blame for the Tiananmen protests. He swiftly grabbed the reins of power, doing battle with a Maoist bureacracy to implement reforms.
His economic policies made him one of the West's favourite communist leaders. He was twice named Time Magazine's Man of the Year.
When he went to the United States in 1979, he delighted his hosts by donning a huge cowboy hat at a rodeo in Texas.
But Deng failed many of China's people, those who dreamt of political reform along with economic liberalisation.
Even before the military moved into Beijing in 1989, many Chinese saw Deng as an old man simply clinging to power.
In May and June of 1989, when hundreds of thousands took to the streets in the biggest anti-government protests since 1949, Deng was lampooned and cursed.
Banners called on him to resign. People smashed bottles in a coded protest, for in Chinese "little bottle" sounds the same as Deng's given name.
The increasingly reclusive Deng resigned in November 1989 as head of the Communist Party's Central Military Commission -- which commands the three-million-strong army.

The following March he stepped down as chairman of the less powerful State Military Commission, his last formal post, to retain only the position of honorary president of the China Bridge Players Association.

Deng had already retired from the party politburo, central committee and central advisory commission at the party's 12th congress in 1987, when he forced many old guard revolutionaries to go with him.
After his retirement Deng disappeared from view for months at a time, but remained the ultimate arbiter of power, manipulating power from behind the scenes like emperors of old.
His last appearance was during the 1994 Chinese lunar new year festivities, when state television showed a frail and faltering 90-year-old inspecting a newly built bridge in Shanghai.
